title: What Is REST?
learning_outcomes: Explain how what is rest? affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from meaning of representational state transfer to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on what is rest? in introduction to rest api development. You will connect meaning of representational state transfer to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: What Is REST? matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying meaning of representational state transfer deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 3 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 3: Meaning of Representational State Transfer → REST as an architectural style → REST versus an API protocol → RESTful APIs versus REST-inspired APIs.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: An API contract describes what a consumer may ask for and what the provider promises to return. In this lesson, treat “What Is REST?” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: What Is REST?
content_blocks.expected_output: A consumer can identify the target resource and requested operation from a documented contract; no implementation language is implied.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Meaning of Representational State Transfer”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “REST as an architectural style” and “RESTful APIs versus REST-inspired APIs”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Start with the problem and the consumer contract before choosing tools. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating what is rest?. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Meaning of Representational State Transfer” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for What Is REST? with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating what is rest? as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: An API contract describes what a consumer may ask for and what the provider promises to return. In this lesson, treat “What Is REST?” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 4: What Is a REST API?.
